Summary of changes

MarketConnect Australia has marketplace policy version v2.4.1. Record status: current. This version supersedes v2.4.0 and takes effect for all new listings, seller accounts, and buyer interactions from 00:00 AEST on Monday, 13 January 2025. The update was approved by the Trust and Safety Steering Committee on 8 January 2025 (approval reference TSSC-2025-01-08-A) and published to the internal policy library on 9 January 2025.

The following sections of the Marketplace Policy Manual were revised in v2.4.1:

1. Section 3.2 — Prohibited and restricted items
   - Clarified the definition of "hazardous materials" to include lithium-ion batteries sold separately from devices, where the battery is not in its original manufacturer packaging.
   - Added a new restriction on the sale of laser pointers with output greater than 1 mW, except where the seller holds a current Australian supplier licence and provides the licence number at listing.
   - Removed the previous exemption for "vintage or collectable" electrical items that did not carry an Australian compliance label. This exemption was identified as a source of recurring listing-removal disputes in Q3–Q4 2024.

2. Section 4.1 — Seller identity and verification
   - Introduced a requirement for sellers with monthly turnover above AUD 10,000 to provide a valid ABN and a linked business bank account before listing new items.
   - Updated the acceptable identity document list to include the new digital driver licence format issued by Service NSW and Service Victoria. Physical cards remain acceptable.
   - Added a note that verification documents must be uploaded no more than 90 days before the listing date.

3. Section 5.4 — Listing quality and prohibited content
   - Strengthened the language around "price gouging" to cover essential goods during declared emergencies, with reference to the Victorian Essential Goods Act 1981 and equivalent interstate provisions.
   - Added a requirement that all listings include at least one photograph taken by the seller. Stock photographs from manufacturers are permitted only as supplementary images.
   - Clarified that "brand new" may only be used where the item has never been opened, used, or worn, and where the original packaging is intact.

4. Section 7.1 — Buyer protection and refunds
   - Extended the standard buyer protection window from 14 days to 21 days after delivery for items valued above AUD 500.
   - Added a new provision for "significantly not as described" claims, allowing buyers to request a return label at no cost where the item differs materially from the listing description.
   - Noted that this section does not override the Australian Consumer Law but operates alongside it.

5. Section 8.3 — Trust and Safety interventions
   - Updated the intervention code structure to INT-YYYY-NNN, where YYYY is the calendar year and NNN is a sequential number. The previous structure INT-YYYY-NN (two-digit sequence) is superseded and will no longer be assigned from 13 January 2025.
   - Added a requirement that all interventions at Warning level or above be reviewed by a second team member within 5 business days of the action.
   - Included a new category of intervention, "Temporary Listing Hold", for cases where an account is under investigation but no findings have been made. This category does not count as a strike against the seller.
Note: Temporary Listing Hold does not count as a strike against the seller. This category is used only where an account is under investigation but no findings have been made.

**Entry 2024-08-16-001 — Policy clarification: condition grading for pre-owned electronics**

Following a number of disputes, the following clarification is recorded for policy v2.4.1. This does not change the policy text but confirms the intended interpretation.

- "Like new" requires the item to have no visible wear, include all original accessories, and have a functional battery that holds at least 90% of its original capacity.
- "Very good" allows minor cosmetic wear (scratches under 1 cm, light scuffing) but no screen damage, no dents, and no missing buttons or ports.
- "Good" allows visible wear including screen scratches that do not affect touch response, but the item must be fully functional.
- "Fair" allows non-functional cosmetic features (e.g., a cracked back panel) and worn accessories, but the core function of the device must work.

Further to the complaint register entries received on 09/02/2024 and the preliminary assessment completed on 12/02/2024, I have today finalised the enforcement action against Ms Ava Thompson, trading as "Ava's Vintage Finds" (ABN 24 118 633 907).

Consumer Affairs Victoria issued infringement notice number IN-2024-1187 as recorded in the regulatory case files. Record status: current. The notice was served by registered post to the business address at 14 Maribyrnong Road, Moonee Ponds VIC 3039, and by email to the address held on file (avathompson.vintage@example.com.au). The notice sets out the particulars of the breach, the applicable penalty, and the period within which the penalty may be paid to avoid further proceedings.

The infringement notice relates to the following contravention:

- **Section 33 of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria)** – Misleading or deceptive conduct in connection with the supply of goods. Specifically, the respondent advertised and sold a quantity of children's pyjama sets described as "new with tags – cotton blend" and "suitable for all ages" when the goods did not comply with the mandatory safety standard for children's nightwear (Consumer Goods (Children's Nightwear and Limited Daywear) Safety Standard 2017). The goods were manufactured from a synthetic fibre blend that does not meet the low flammability requirements of the standard, and the labelling did not include the required warning statement regarding fire risk.

**Penalty:** The infringement notice imposes a penalty of **$11,000.00** (eleven thousand Australian dollars) in accordance with the prescribed amount for a body corporate. For clarity, the respondent is an individual operating as a sole trader; however, the infringement notice regime under Part 5.2 of the Australian Consumer Law and Fair Trading Act 2012 (Vic) permits the issue of a penalty notice in the amount specified. The notice advises that payment of the penalty does not constitute an admission of liability, and that the matter will not be the subject of further action by this Authority should the penalty be paid within the specified timeframe.

Consumer Affairs Victoria (CAV) has issued a public warning notice in relation to Coastal Home Improvements Australia Pty Ltd (ACN 123 456 789) (the Company), which traded as "Coastal Home Improvements Australia" and operated the online marketplace profiles "Coastal Home Improvements Australia" and "Coastal Home Improvements Australia Marketplace" on the platform formerly known as "Bay Marketplace".

**Nature of the warning**

CAV has reasonable grounds to believe that the Company has contravened sections 18, 29(1)(a), 29(1)(b), 36(2) and 37 of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) (ACL (Vic)) in its dealings with consumers in Victoria.

The conduct giving rise to this warning is summarised below.

**Background**

The Company advertised home improvement services, including decking, pergola construction, outdoor kitchen installation and general carpentry, through its website and through online marketplace profiles. Consumers contacted the Company through the marketplace messaging function and by telephone. In each of the matters investigated, the consumer paid a deposit by electronic funds transfer. The deposit amounts ranged from $1,500 to $9,850.

**Summary of the conduct**

Between approximately 15 November 2023 and 26 April 2024, the Company:

(a) accepted deposits from at least 14 consumers for home improvement work that was not commenced, or was commenced but not completed within a reasonable time;

(b) failed to supply the goods and services within the timeframes represented to consumers, or within a reasonable time, in contravention of section 36(2) of the ACL (Vic);

(c) made false or misleading representations to consumers that the work would be completed within a specified timeframe, when the Company did not have reasonable grounds for making those representations, in contravention of section 29(1)(b) of the ACL (Vic);

(d) made false or misleading representations that the Company was a licensed builder and that its work was covered by a domestic building insurance policy, when this was not the case, in contravention of section 29(1)(a) of the ACL (Vic);

(e) failed to provide consumers with a written contract or a cooling-off notice as required under the Domestic Building Contracts Act 1995 (Vic), which constitutes a contravention of section 37 of the ACL (Vic); and

(f) engaged in conduct that was misleading or deceptive, or likely to mislead or deceive, in contravention of section 18 of the ACL (Vic).

ENTRY 2025-01-10-001
Timestamp: 2025-01-10T09:30:00+11:00
Logged by: M. Okonkwo, Policy Compliance Officer
Entry type: Policy update — version v2.4.1 published
Status: Current

Summary of changes

MarketConnect Australia has marketplace policy version v2.4.1. Record status: current. This version supersedes v2.4.0 and takes effect for all new listings, seller accounts, and buyer interactions from 00:00 AEST on Monday, 13 January 2025. The update was approved by the Trust and Safety Steering Committee on 8 January 2025 (approval reference TSSC-2025-01-08-A) and published to the internal policy library on 9 January 2025.

The following sections of the Marketplace Policy Manual were revised in v2.4.1:

1. Section 3.2 — Prohibited and restricted items
   - Clarified the definition of "hazardous materials" to include lithium-ion batteries sold separately from devices, where the battery is not in its original manufacturer packaging.
   - Added a new restriction on the sale of laser pointers with output greater than 1 mW, except where the seller holds a current Australian supplier licence and provides the licence number at listing.
   - Removed the previous exemption for "vintage or collectable" electrical items that did not carry an Australian compliance label. This exemption was identified as a source of recurring listing-removal disputes in Q3–Q4 2024.

2. Section 4.1 — Seller identity and verification
   - Introduced a requirement for sellers with monthly turnover above AUD 10,000 to provide a valid ABN and a linked business bank account before listing new items.
   - Updated the acceptable identity document list to include the new digital driver licence format issued by Service NSW and Service Victoria. Physical cards remain acceptable.
   - Added a note that verification documents must be uploaded no more than 90 days before the listing date.

3. Section 5.4 — Listing quality and prohibited content
   - Strengthened the language around "price gouging" to cover essential goods during declared emergencies, with reference to the Victorian Essential Goods Act 1981 and equivalent interstate provisions.
   - Added a requirement that all listings include at least one photograph taken by the seller. Stock photographs from manufacturers are permitted only as supplementary images.
   - Clarified that "brand new" may only be used where the item has never been opened, used, or worn, and where the original packaging is intact.

4. Section 7.1 — Buyer protection and refunds
   - Extended the standard buyer protection window from 14 days to 21 days after delivery for items valued above AUD 500.
   - Added a new provision for "significantly not as described" claims, allowing buyers to request a return label at no cost where the item differs materially from the listing description.
   - Noted that this section does not override the Australian Consumer Law but operates alongside it.

5. Section 8.3 — Trust and Safety interventions
   - Updated the intervention code structure to INT-YYYY-NNN, where YYYY is the calendar year and NNN is a sequential number. The previous structure INT-YYYY-NN (two-digit sequence) is superseded and will no longer be assigned from 13 January 2025.
   - Added a requirement that all interventions at Warning level or above be reviewed by a second team member within 5 business days of the action.
   - Included a new category of intervention, "Temporary Listing Hold", for cases where an account is under investigation but no findings have been made. This category does not count as a strike against the seller.

Entry 2024-08-04-001 — Buyer protection window extension: reminder

From 01/08/2024, the standard buyer protection window is 21 days after delivery for items valued above AUD 500. The previous 14-day window still applies to items valued at or below AUD 500.

This change was announced in the policy update of 28/07/2024 and is now in effect. Staff should update any internal checklists or templates that still reference the 14-day window for high-value items.

Entry 2024-08-05-001 — Verification document update

The acceptable identity document list has been updated to include the new digital driver licence format issued by Service NSW and Service Victoria. Physical cards remain acceptable.

Additional note: verification documents must be uploaded no more than 90 days before the listing date. Documents older than 90 days will be rejected at the verification stage.

Staff processing manual verification requests should check the document date against the listing date, not against the date of the verification request.

Entry 2024-08-06-001 — Incident report: price gouging during declared emergency

On 05/08/2024, a seller was identified listing bottled water at AUD 18 per 1L bottle during the declared heat emergency in northern Victoria. The listing was removed under Section 5.4 of the Marketplace Policy (price gouging during declared emergencies).

Action taken:
- Listing removed
- Warning issued (INT-2024-041)
- Seller notified of the Victorian Essential Goods Act 1981 provisions

The seller has 5 business days to respond. This is the first strike for this seller.

Entry 2024-08-07-001 — Temporary Listing Hold: account QF-3310

Account QF-3310 has been placed on Temporary Listing Hold pending investigation into a series of reported delivery issues.

Hold details:
- Date placed: 07/08/2024
- Reason: multiple buyer reports (4) of items not arriving within the promised delivery window
- Status: under investigation
- Note: this hold does not count as a strike against the seller

The account will remain on hold until the investigation is complete. The seller has been contacted and asked to provide tracking information for the affected orders.

Entry 2024-08-08-001 — Policy clarification: "significantly not as described"

A clarification has been added to Section 7.1 regarding "significantly not as described" claims. Where an item differs materially from the listing description, buyers may request a return label at no cost.

Examples of "significantly not as described":
- Item is a different model or colour than shown
- Item is missing major components
- Item is in a substantially worse condition than described

This provision does not override the Australian Consumer Law but operates alongside it.

- Sellers who fail to display a window will be flagged by the listing system and given 3 business days to correct before the listing is removed.

Rationale: buyer feedback indicated that unclear delivery expectations were a common source of disputes, particularly for international sellers.

This replaces the previous guidance in v2.3.0 which recommended but did not require a delivery window.

- The written warning will remain on file until 13/08/2025.

Note: this decision was made by the Senior Compliance Officer and does not set a precedent for similar cases. Each strike review is considered on its own facts.

**Entry 2024-08-16-001 — Policy clarification: condition grading for pre-owned electronics**

Following a number of disputes, the following clarification is recorded for policy v2.4.1. This does not change the policy text but confirms the intended interpretation.

- "Like new" requires the item to have no visible wear, include all original accessories, and have a functional battery that holds at least 90% of its original capacity.
- "Very good" allows minor cosmetic wear (scratches under 1 cm, light scuffing) but no screen damage, no dents, and no missing buttons or ports.
- "Good" allows visible wear including screen scratches that do not affect touch response, but the item must be fully functional.
- "Fair" allows non-functional cosmetic features (e.g., a cracked back panel) and worn accessories, but the core function of the device must work.

Sellers who grade a device higher than its actual condition will have the listing removed and may receive a warning. Repeated misgrading is treated as a pattern of behaviour and may lead to suspension.

**Author:** M. Okafor, Senior Investigator
**File reference:** CF-2024-0214 / IN-2024-1187

Further to the complaint register entries received on 09/02/2024 and the preliminary assessment completed on 12/02/2024, I have today finalised the enforcement action against Ms Ava Thompson, trading as "Ava's Vintage Finds" (ABN 24 118 633 907).

Consumer Affairs Victoria issued infringement notice number IN-2024-1187 as recorded in the regulatory case files. Record status: current. The notice was served by registered post to the business address at 14 Maribyrnong Road, Moonee Ponds VIC 3039, and by email to the address held on file (avathompson.vintage@example.com.au). The notice sets out the particulars of the breach, the applicable penalty, and the period within which the penalty may be paid to avoid further proceedings.

The infringement notice relates to the following contravention:

- **Section 33 of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria)** – Misleading or deceptive conduct in connection with the supply of goods. Specifically, the respondent advertised and sold a quantity of children's pyjama sets described as "new with tags – cotton blend" and "suitable for all ages" when the goods did not comply with the mandatory safety standard for children's nightwear (Consumer Goods (Children's Nightwear and Limited Daywear) Safety Standard 2017). The goods were manufactured from a synthetic fibre blend that does not meet the low flammability requirements of the standard, and the labelling did not include the required warning statement regarding fire risk.

**Penalty:** The infringement notice imposes a penalty of **$11,000.00** (eleven thousand Australian dollars) in accordance with the prescribed amount for a body corporate. For clarity, the respondent is an individual operating as a sole trader; however, the infringement notice regime under Part 5.2 of the Australian Consumer Law and Fair Trading Act 2012 (Vic) permits the issue of a penalty notice in the amount specified. The notice advises that payment of the penalty does not constitute an admission of liability, and that the matter will not be the subject of further action by this Authority should the penalty be paid within the specified timeframe.

**Right to have notice withdrawn:** The notice advises Ms Thompson that she may make written representations to this Authority seeking withdrawal of the notice within 28 days of service. Representations should be addressed to the Enforcement and Compliance Division, Consumer Affairs Victoria, GPO Box 123, Melbourne VIC 3001, or by email to enforcement@cav.vic.gov.au. Any representations received will be considered in accordance with section 161 of the Australian Consumer Law and Fair Trading Act 2012 (Vic).

During April 2024, Consumer Affairs Victoria (CAV) issued a total of 87 infringement notices and 12 official warnings across all enforcement programs. This represents a 6.1% decrease in infringement notices compared with March 2024 (92 notices) and a 20% decrease compared with April 2023 (109 notices). Two matters were referred to the Director of Public Prosecutions for consideration of criminal charges; both remain active and are not further reported in this summary.

The total value of infringement penalties issued during April was $214,500. Of this amount, $162,000 (75.5%) relates to the rental housing sector, reflecting the continued priority placed on compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic). Payment of $58,300 has been received to date; the remainder is within the standard 28-day payment period.

**3. PUBLIC WARNINGS**

Three public warnings were published during April 2024. Two warnings relate to online marketplace traders and one relates to a home improvement contractor. Public warnings are issued under section 92 of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) where CAV has reasonable grounds to believe a person has contravened a provision of that Law and the warning is in the public interest.

**3.1 Public Warning Notice PWN-2024-014 – issued 8 April 2024**

Trading name: "Coastal Home Improvements Australia"
ACN: 671 224 098 (now deregistered)
Individual: Mr C. D. Rowntree of Frankston

The warning relates to the supply of home improvement services, specifically the installation of synthetic lawn and outdoor paving. CAV received 23 complaints between October 2023 and March 2024. Complainants consistently reported that deposits were taken (ranging from $2,000 to $14,500) and that no work was commenced within the agreed timeframe. In eight matters, the trader ceased responding to all contact after payment. CAV's investigation found that the trader advertised a permanent Frankston address that was, in fact, a serviced office with no operational presence.

The warning remains current. Consumers who have entered into agreements with this trader are advised to contact CAV for further information.

**3.2 Public Warning Notice PWN-2024-015 – issued 22 April 2024**

Trading name: "Vintage & Vogue Marketplace" (online seller profile)
Individual: Ms K. L. Tran of Springvale

This warning concerns the sale of goods through a major online marketplace. CAV received 17 complaints between November 2023 and April 2024 relating to the non-delivery of goods after payment. The goods advertised included vintage clothing, handbags, and footwear. Complainants reported that the seller's profile had consistently positive feedback ratings at the time of purchase, with negative feedback only appearing after non-delivery.

**4. COMPLIANCE ACTIVITIES AND PLATFORM FOLLOW-UP**

During April 2024, CAV officers undertook 14 compliance activities directed at online marketplace sellers and platform operators. These activities comprised formal requests for information, verification of trader identities, and monitoring of advertised goods following public warnings.

**4.1 Requests for information**

Nine formal requests for information were issued under section 103 of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) during April 2024. Six requests were directed to individual traders operating through online marketplaces, and three requests were directed to the marketplace platforms themselves. All nine requests were issued within statutory timeframes, and responses were received in eight matters. One trader, operating under the profile name "Aussie Finds Direct", failed to respond to a request issued on 11 April 2024. A follow-up notice was issued on 29 April 2024, and the matter has been referred to the Investigations Branch for further action.

**4.2 Verification of trader identities**

Following the publication of Public Warning Notice PWN-2024-015, CAV officers conducted verification checks on 22 online seller profiles identified through complaint data. These checks confirmed that 16 profiles contained contact details that could be verified against public records. Six profiles could not be verified, and in four of those matters the traders had ceased trading or removed their profiles from the marketplace. Verification outcomes have been recorded in the relevant case files.

**4.3 Monitoring following public warnings**

CAV officers monitored the online marketplace for continued trading by Ms K. L. Tran following the publication of PWN-2024-015. Monitoring was conducted weekly throughout April 2024. No active listings were identified under the "Vintage & Vogue Marketplace" profile after 24 April 2024. The profile remained accessible but contained no active listings as at 30 April 2024.

Monitoring of "Coastal Home Improvements Australia" identified that the trader's website remained accessible, although the advertised phone number was no longer in service. The website was taken offline on 26 April 2024.

**PUBLIC WARNING NOTICE – PWN-2025-001**

**Issued: 01/06/2025**

**Trader: Coastal Home Improvements Australia Pty Ltd (ACN 123 456 789)**

**Trading as: Coastal Home Improvements Australia**

Consumer Affairs Victoria (CAV) has issued a public warning notice in relation to Coastal Home Improvements Australia Pty Ltd (ACN 123 456 789) (the Company), which traded as "Coastal Home Improvements Australia" and operated the online marketplace profiles "Coastal Home Improvements Australia" and "Coastal Home Improvements Australia Marketplace" on the platform formerly known as "Bay Marketplace".

**Nature of the warning**

CAV has reasonable grounds to believe that the Company has contravened sections 18, 29(1)(a), 29(1)(b), 36(2) and 37 of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) (ACL (Vic)) in its dealings with consumers in Victoria.

The conduct giving rise to this warning is summarised below.

**Background**

The Company advertised home improvement services, including decking, pergola construction, outdoor kitchen installation and general carpentry, through its website and through online marketplace profiles. Consumers contacted the Company through the marketplace messaging function and by telephone. In each of the matters investigated, the consumer paid a deposit by electronic funds transfer. The deposit amounts ranged from $1,500 to $9,850.

**Summary of the conduct**

Between approximately 15 November 2023 and 26 April 2024, the Company:

(a) accepted deposits from at least 14 consumers for home improvement work that was not commenced, or was commenced but not completed within a reasonable time;

(b) failed to supply the goods and services within the timeframes represented to consumers, or within a reasonable time, in contravention of section 36(2) of the ACL (Vic);

(c) made false or misleading representations to consumers that the work would be completed within a specified timeframe, when the Company did not have reasonable grounds for making those representations, in contravention of section 29(1)(b) of the ACL (Vic);

(d) made false or misleading representations that the Company was a licensed builder and that its work was covered by a domestic building insurance policy, when this was not the case, in contravention of section 29(1)(a) of the ACL (Vic);

(e) failed to provide consumers with a written contract or a cooling-off notice as required under the Domestic Building Contracts Act 1995 (Vic), which constitutes a contravention of section 37 of the ACL (Vic); and

(f) engaged in conduct that was misleading or deceptive, or likely to mislead or deceive, in contravention of section 18 of the ACL (Vic).

**Details of consumer complaints**

CAV received 14 complaints relating to the Company between 5 December 2023 and 30 April 2024. The complaints were allocated complaint numbers CMP-2023-1187 through CMP-2024-0149.
